title: Version-lock placement policy playbook
body:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for how 'version-lock' directives from the model registry should interact with placement and routing decisions in a multi-region control plane. Goal: capture pragmatic rules, a compact compatibility matrix we can program against, and an operational checklist for rollout/fallback scenarios.

Context and motivation:
- Engineering teams want two capabilities: 1) guarantee a specific model binary is used for a given customer/route (regulatory, quality), and 2) keep routing flexible so we can meet latency and capacity SLOs across regions.
- Existing pin/pinning docs have a lot of good edge-case discussion; this doc focuses on the translation layer between registry 'version-lock' metadata and the orchestrator placement/routing heuristics.
- Working assumption: control plane holds authoritative mapping of version-lock -> serving affinities, but can apply configurable constraints (region-only, hardware-agnostic, strict/soft).

Key terms (working):
- version-lock: registry flag indicating requests for X should use model:foo:vNN exactly (no automatic substitutions).
- soft-lock: prefer vNN, but allow compatible fallback variants if strict capacity/latency breach.
- placement policy: the combination of region, perf-tier (gpu-type), and capacity-band used to select a serving host.
- compatibility class: categorical compatibility between versions/variants (see matrix).

Requirements (non-exhaustive):
- If a customer has legal/regulatory requirement -> enforcement must be strict (no substitution).
- If the reason is quality (A/B test or regression), allow controlled canaries before changing default fallback behavior.
- Control-plane must expose diagnostics explaining why a request was routed to an alternate variant.

Decision variables we need to encode in the control plane: (configurable per-tenant)
- enforcement-level: strict | soft | advisory
- region-strictness: global | region-restricted | region-preferred
- hw-strictness: exact | family-compatible | any
- kv-cache-affinity: require-cache-warm | allow-remote-cache | rebuild-on-demand

Compatibility matrix (compact ASCII; rows = requested version attributes, cols = candidate serving variants):
Note: this is a canonicalization we can represent as bitflags in code.

| Requested | Candidate: same-version | Candidate: patch-compatible | Candidate: arch-compatible | Candidate: quantized-8 | Candidate: different-arch |
|-----------|----------------------:|-----------------------:|----------------------:|-------------------:|--------------------:|
| exact-binary   | YES                   | NO                    | NO                   | NO                | NO                 |
| semver-minor-compatible | PREFER                | YES                   | MAYBE                | MAYBE             | NO                 |
| api-stable    | PREFER                | MAYBE                 | YES                  | MAYBE             | NO                 |
| behavior-eval-locked | STRICT                | NO                    | NO                   | NO                | NO                 |
| hw-agnostic   | YES                   | YES                   | YES                  | MAYBE             | MAYBE              |

Legend: YES = allowed without extra approval; PREFER = allowed but prefer same-version if available; MAYBE = allowed only under soft-lock or if explicitly permitted by tenant settings; NO = disallowed.

How this maps to routing heuristics (sketch):
1) Evaluate tenant-level enforcement-level. If strict -> only candidates marked YES for that request category. If none -> return 412 error (or configurable fallback policy).
2) If soft -> build ordered candidate list: same-version (if available in region) -> patch-compatible -> arch-compatible -> quantized variants in same region -> cross-region same-version -> cross-region patch-compatible.
3) Account for kv-cache-affinity: if request has high cache-hit dependency (large autocomplete sessions), prefer nodes with warm KV cache even if it means selecting patch-compatible variants, unless tenant has behavior-eval-locked.
4) When selecting cross-region: respect region-strictness preferences; add routing cost penalty (latency) to candidate score.

Routing decision example (pseudo-flow):
- Input: request tagged model:foo:v13, tenant enforcement=soft, region=eu-west
- In-region same-version capacity = 0 (exhausted)
- In-region patch-compatible (v12) capacity = available and flagged PREFER
- Decision: choose v12 in-region if performance delta < tenant threshold; otherwise check cross-region v13 and weigh network latency vs model delta.

Operational failure modes and mitigations (notes):
- Failure mode: strict-lock + region-strictness + sudden capacity loss -> 412 errors or dropped traffic.
  Mitigation: preconfigured 'emergency-override' policy (tenant opt-in) that can temporarily relax region constraint to restore availability and create async ticket to CS.
- Failure mode: soft-lock misconfig + hidden behavior change after patch release -> regressions in production.
  Mitigation: require model onboarding to supply a small suite of regression prompts and a 'change severity' label. Soft-lock falls back only if change severity <= threshold.
- Failure mode: kv cache warmness mismatch when routing across variant types -> huge latency variance.
  Mitigation: metric-based gating: if median tail latency across last 10m jumps > 2x baseline after fallback, automatically revert routing for active sessions.

Local developer checklist (for platform eng and solutions):
- [ ] Add version-lock metadata parsing in registry sync job (INF-3421).
- [ ] Implement enforcement-level and region-strictness flags in control plane API (PATCH api/v1/tenants/:id/policies).
- [ ] Add compatibility class function in serving-runtime to return bitflags for candidate matching.
- [ ] Expose routing reasoning trace in request metadata (route.trace_reason, route.candidate_score).
- [ ] Write e2e tests that simulate capacity exhaustion and measure fallback choices.
- [ ] Create metric dashboard: "version-lock_fallback_rate" and "version-lock_block_rate" per tenant.

Rollout plan (staged):
- alpha: internal-only tenants, enforcement-level=advisory -> collect route traces and metrics for 2 weeks.
- beta: enable soft for small external tenants with opt-in and CS awareness.
- GA: default enforcement-level=soft, strict only by explicit contract; strict-for-regulatory enabled via req.

Open questions / TODOs (short):
- How do we represent multi-model ensembles with mixed-version components? (e.g., encoder v1 + decoder v2)
- Should quantized variants be considered 'compatible' when the tenant has accuracy SLOs? Add explicit quantization-allowed flag on tenant config.
- UI: how much detail should Console surface vs. hidden heuristics? (console column: "routing reason" vs full trace).
- Telemetry attribution: can we reliably attribute a regression to fallback variant vs. model drift? Need controlled evaluation harness.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic — we prefer a small set of orthogonal knobs (enforcement-level, region/hw strictness, kv-cache-affinity) instead of a combinatorial policy language at first cut.
- The compatibility matrix should be compact and serializable; implementation idea: store 8-bit bitmask per candidate where bits correspond to categories (binary-match, patch-compat, arch-compat, quant-compat, cache-sensitive).
- If you have concrete tenant examples that require alternative behavior, add them to linked_artifacts and we'll iterate.

References and context links:
- INF-3421 (registry metadata migration) -> https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/INF-3421
- PR for candidate scoring prototype -> https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987
- Console tracing discussion (notes) -> confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Placement+Policy+Draft

Last quick thought: treat version-lock as a 'contract' with three states: advisory (observability only), soft (prefer but allow fallbacks), strict (only exact fulfills contract). The control plane must make that contract visible in metrics and traces so CS and customers understand impact.

-- Evan
(Working draft, will iterate after internal review)
